title: Hot-path fallback cost tabletop and dependency heatmap workshop
summary: Internal tabletop focused on failure modes for the hot path during launch traffic, cost delta for fallback strategies, and a dependency heatmap to identify brittle components. Decided on a three-tier fallback plan, a short pilot for KV cache aggressive warming, and a follow-up benchmarking run next week. Action items assigned for SRE, Runtime, and Product to produce numbers and a small runbook.
topics: fallback strategy (model downgrade, region failover, degraded features)
dependency heatmap and single points of failure
KV cache warming and eviction policies
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-02 09:00 PT
Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Priya, Carlos, Liam, Sofia, Alex, Jenna, Tom

[00:00] Maya: okay let's kick off, uh, thanks everyone for hopping on. goal for today is a tabletop for hot path failures at launch — we want concrete fallback options and cost deltas so launch can decide go/no-go.

[00:18] Ethan: quick note, i pushed the dep heatmap to the shared drive, link in the chat. it's rough, but shows where we have single-region KV and the new quant kernel rollout.

[00:35] Priya: thanks, i saw that. oncall's biggest worry is KV cold misses under spike, that combined with the kernel compilation jitter could push p99 over the SLO.

[00:52] Liam: comp jitter is real, particularly when we hit new sequence lengths. we have heuristics to preselect kernels but cold starts still happen on rare shapes,  especially with mixed-quant variants.

[01:10] Carlos: can we frame the fallback tiers before we simulate? what are we comfortable with for automatic downgrade?

[01:22] Maya: my thought — three tiers: 1) graceful degraded output (shorter generation, stop non-critical plugins), 2) model variant fallback (quantized or smaller model), 3) region/burst fallback to dedicated capacity or queue. need cost numbers for tiers 2 and 3.

[01:40] Sofia: i can simulate output degradation impact on NPS/quality metrics with our eval set; shorter generation tends to lose context in a small slice, but not catastrophic for most templates.

[01:58] Jenna: from ops, tier 1 is best — it's cheap and quick, but some customers will see functional regression. tier 3 is expensive — shifting to dedicated pools adds linear GPU-hours and we should show the $$ delta.

[02:18] Tom: also let's not forget audit/logging costs — more retries and fallbacks increase token counts and audit events. auditor/customer legal will ask.

[02:35] Ethan: ok let's run through a failure scenario: sudden 3x traffic spike in us-west, kv hit drops by 40%, kernel jitter increases p99 by ~80ms. what sequence?

[02:50] Priya: immediate mitigation is prefix caching prewarmed for top 50 templates, which reduces remote misses. but warming has memory cost and eviction pressure.

[03:07] Liam: also we can enable continuous micro-batching to smooth spikes but it adds latency tail for single requests — tradeoff.

[03:25] Maya: right, we need numbers. can we estimate cost impact for: a) enabling model-variant fallback to 13B quant, and b) bursting to dedicated 8-GPU pool for 15 minutes?

[03:40] Ethan: rough calc — if we move 20% of tokens to 13B quant, we save ~50% per-token compute cost on those tokens. but there's quality drop. for dedicated burst, 8x A100-hours for 15 minutes equals 2 GPU-hours, which is about $X in our current pricing table. i'll convert to run-rate delta.

[04:01] Sofia: i'll run an eval comparing our prod prompt set against 13B quant outputs and flag regressions; we should surface prompts with high sensitivity.

[04:15] Carlos: dependency heatmap — which components are red? Ethan, you noted single-region KV and the shard manager for routings?

[04:27] Ethan: yes: KV store in us-west (critical), shard manager (control-plane) in primary region, and a telemetry pipeline that if backpressured will slow autoscaling signals.

[04:40] Priya: so a control-plane outage could prevent rolling fallback policies from triggering. we need a low-latency emergency switch that doesn't rely on the metric pipeline — maybe an oncall flip that enacts canned routing rules.

[04:58] Jenna: oncall flip is doable but needs a tested runbook. we don't want manual steps under pager stress. can we automate a safe-mode that toggles the three tiers automatically?

[05:12] Liam: automation is possible if we define simple SLO-derived triggers: e.g., 5m sustained p99>300ms -> enable tier1; sustained 10m -> tier2. but metric noise and flapping are a concern. we need hysteresis and cooldowns.

[05:36] Maya: note to team: hysteresis thresholds need to be conservative. we'll table exact numbers but agree on the 5/10 minute windows for now.

[05:45] Tom: regarding cost presentation to launch stakeholders, show three columns: latency impact, functional impact, and incremental cost ($/min) per tier. they want easy comparators.

[06:00] Ethan: agreed. i'll produce a spreadsheet with the incremental GPU-hour and token counts.

[06:10] Sofia: another quick point on KV warming — we can prewarm top templates but what about cold long-tail? warm-as-you-go plus predictive prefetch using historical routes might cover 80%.

[06:25] Priya: predictive prefetch increases network and IO cost; also risk of read amplification. need numbers.

[06:40] Maya: okay let's run a short tabletop script. scenario A: KV degrade + kernel jitter. Who plays ops? Jenna, you and Priya run this.

[06:52] Jenna: yes, we'll run it. action — simulate 40% kv miss and toggle kernel jitter.

[07:00] [simulation silence ~ brief pause]

[07:12] Jenna: initial detection — p99 spiked to 420ms, rate steady. we enabled tier1 (shorter generations) at 4m. quality complaints started to appear after 8m on 2 prompts.

[07:33] Priya: autoscaler delayed, telemetry queued. control-plane alert fired but auto-runbook didn't kick because of missing heartbeat from shard manager.

[07:47] Liam: at 12m we triggered tier2 in the sim — model variant fallback — latency dropped to 310ms but eval shows 13% drop in answer correctness on a subset.

[08:02] Tom: cost numbers from the sim: tier1 incremental token count + retries added ~15% token cost; tier2 saved GPU cycles but increased downstream tokenization overhead; tier3 would have cost ~ $Y for the 15-minute burst. (note: actual $ numbers to be filled).

[08:22] Maya: good. so decision logic: prefer tier1+prewarm for short blips, drop to tier2 for sustained events >10m, only use tier3 if we detect region-wide capacity saturation or regulatory required isolation.

[08:40] Sofia: i'll annotate eval outputs highlighting high-impact prompts and produce a heatmap of prompt sensitivity.

[08:49] Ethan: follow-up — we need a small benchmark run that simulates 2x/3x spikes with KV miss patterns and runs the fallback logic end-to-end. estimate 4 hours to run and analyze.

[09:02] Priya: SRE will set up the benchmark harness; we need the dataset (Sofia) and the config for fallback toggles (Liam/Ethan).

[09:12] Maya: okay assign those. one more item: compliance and audit log growth if we enable more fallbacks/redo. Tom and Carlos, flag any legal/audit concerns.

[09:23] Carlos: legal will ask about PII retention during retries and any extra telemetry forwarded to third-party log stores. we should propose redaction and retention caps.

[09:34] Tom: also note potential vendor cost when bursting to dedicated — counters on marketplace fees. will get precise numbers.

[09:45] Maya: wrap up — high-level consensus on three-tier plan with conservative thresholds, runway to run a 4-hour benchmark next week, and deliver a short launch-facing one-pager with numbers.

[09:58] Jenna: oncall will draft an emergency flip runbook and a stub automation repo for hysteresis-based toggles.

[10:08] Ethan: i'll own the spreadsheet with cost deltas and the dep heatmap update.

[10:18] Maya: perfect, thanks all. meeting adjourned.
